newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-WMC says interested in CVRD stake.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-WMC says interested in CVRD stake.

text.p: Australian-based resources group WMC Ltd on Friday confirmed a newspaper report that it was interested in taking a stake in Brazil's state-owned mining firm CVRD but said it had not entered any negotiations.

"We've registered to have a look at the (CVRD) data room but we haven't been in there yet and we haven't formed any partnerships...There's a lot of water to go under the bridge," WMC spokesman Geoff Kelly told Reuters.
The so-called data room contained confidential information which would allow WMC to assess whether it would be able to make a bid, Kelly said.
The Australian newspaper said on Friday WMC was negotiating to join a possible US$5 billion joint venture to buy a 45 percent interest in Companhia Vale de Rio Doce (CRVD).
"WMC has a team negotiating in Brazil which could result in the Australian mining house making an investment of more than US$1 billion," the newspaper said. It did not cite any sources.

Kelly said WMC would have to join a consortium to make a bid and had been approached by number of interested firms, including South African-based Minorco and Gencor Ltd, but no agreements had been struck.
"Everybody over there is aware that we're interested so we've had a lot of people come calling on us," he said.
Kelly declined to comment on the value of the CVRD stake or the possible size of WMC's investment.

Last week, the Brazilian government delayed the sale of the voting stake to April this year from the first quarter to allow independent analysts to evaluate new gold and copper finds before the government sets CVRD's base price.

The latest hiccup in the sale of the world's largest iron ore exporter came after a deluge of reports about "historic" finds in Carajas in Para state, near the existing Igarape Bahia gold mine and the Salobo gold, copper and silver project.
Politicians opposed to the CVRD sell-off and newspapers also said Carajas could significantly alter the value of the company, an assertion some government officials conceded was possible.
The government last week hastened to reassure markets politics did not play a role in the decision to delay CVRD's privatization.
The asset sale is expected to begin with a block sale of 40-45 percent of voting shares, followed by an internal offer to employees and then a public offering.
WMC's Kelly said the company was examining a number of investment options around the world including the CVRD stake.
"We do this all the time. This isn't unusual. We continually look at an awful lot of options," he said.
